chapter.title: Design Consistent Hashing
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.primary_goal: Understand why naïve modulo-based hashing causes large-scale remapping when servers change, and learn how consistent hashing, hash rings, clockwise lookup, virtual nodes, and affected-key ranges reduce redistribution while improving horizontal scalability and load balance.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 5 begins with the rehashing problem created by the common mapping serverIndex = hash(key) % N. This approach works while the server pool remains fixed, but adding or removing a server changes N and therefore remaps many keys, producing cache misses and unnecessary data movement. Consistent hashing replaces direct modulo mapping with a hash ring. Servers and keys are mapped onto the ring, and a key belongs to the first server encountered when moving clockwise from the key. Adding or removing a server therefore affects only a fraction of keys. The chapter then explains two limitations of the basic ring—uneven partition sizes and non-uniform key distribution—and introduces virtual nodes to improve balance. It concludes by showing how to determine the affected key range when membership changes and summarizes the technique's benefits and real-world use.
chapter_summary.core_problem: Traditional modulo hashing tightly couples key placement to the total number of servers. When N changes, most key-to-server mappings can change even though only one server was added or removed.
chapter_summary.core_solution: Map servers and keys into a common circular hash space. A key is assigned to the first server encountered clockwise. Membership changes then only remap keys in a neighboring portion of the ring rather than nearly the entire keyspace.
major_benefits: Minimizes key redistribution when servers are added or removed.
Makes horizontal scaling easier because data can be distributed more evenly.
Helps mitigate hotspot-key problems by spreading data more evenly.

rehashing_problem.where_N_means: Number of servers in the server pool.

server_failure_example.consequence: Most keys move to different server indexes, not only the keys that were on the failed server. Cache clients then look on the wrong servers and create a storm of cache misses.

consistent_hashing_definition.source_definition_summary: When a hash table is resized under consistent hashing, only about k/n keys need to be remapped on average, where k is the number of keys and n is the number of slots, instead of nearly all keys being remapped.

hash_space.description: All possible SHA-1 hash values lie within this range.

hash_space_and_ring.ring_construction: Conceptually connect the two ends of the linear hash space to form a ring.

servers.rule: Hash each server's IP address or server name with the same hash function and place it on the ring.

keys.rule: Hash each key and place it somewhere on the ring.
keys.important_difference_from_modulo_hashing: There is no modulo operation in the consistent-hashing lookup described here.

lookup.rule: Starting at the key's position, move clockwise until the first server is encountered.

add_server.principle: Only a fraction of keys need redistribution.

chapter_example.reason: server4 becomes the first server encountered clockwise from key0.

remove_server.principle: Only a small fraction of keys need redistribution.

basic_approach_problems.definition: A partition is the hash-space interval between adjacent servers.
basic_approach_problems.why_it_happens: Adding or removing servers makes it impossible to keep all server partitions exactly the same size.
basic_approach_problems.chapter_example: After s1 is removed, s2's partition becomes twice as large as s0's and s3's partitions.

basic_approach_problems.why_it_happens: Server positions can leave large and small intervals, concentrating many keys under one server while others receive few or none.
basic_approach_problems.chapter_example: Most keys can end up on server2 while server1 and server3 have no data.

virtual_nodes.definition: A virtual node refers to a real node; each real server is represented by multiple virtual positions on the hash ring.

example.note: The chapter says 3 is arbitrary and real systems typically use many more virtual nodes.

virtual_nodes.lookup_rule: Move clockwise from the key and use the first virtual node encountered; that virtual node points to its real server.
virtual_nodes.example_lookup: k0 encounters virtual node s1_1 first, so k0 is stored on server1.
why_it_helps: Each server owns multiple partitions distributed around the ring.
Increasing the number of virtual nodes makes key distribution more balanced.
More virtual nodes reduce the standard deviation of load distribution.

quantitative_example_from_source.100_virtual_nodes: Standard deviation around 10% of the mean.
quantitative_example_from_source.200_virtual_nodes: Standard deviation around 5% of the mean.
quantitative_example_from_source.interpretation: More virtual nodes reduce variation and improve balance.

virtual_nodes.tradeoff: More virtual nodes improve balance but require more space to store virtual-node metadata.

method: Start at the newly added server's position.
Move anticlockwise until the previous server is found.
The keys in that interval are the affected keys.
Start at the removed server's former position.
Move anticlockwise until the previous server is found.
The keys in that interval are affected.
when_removing_server.destination: Redistribute those keys to s2, the next server clockwise after the removed node.

key_concepts.definition: Maps a key to serverIndex = hash(key) % N.
When N changes, many keys receive different server indexes, causing widespread remapping.
A hashing approach designed so resizing the server set remaps only a fraction of keys rather than nearly all keys.
The complete output range of the hash function.
A circular representation of the hash space formed by conceptually connecting its two endpoints.
The key-assignment rule: from a key's position, move clockwise until the first server or virtual node is found.
The hash-space interval between adjacent servers on the ring.
A virtual position on the hash ring that represents a real server.
A measure used in the chapter to describe how spread out the load/data distribution is; lower values indicate more balanced distribution.
The interval of the ring whose keys must move after a server is added or removed.

flashcards.front: Why is consistent hashing useful in horizontally scaled systems?
flashcards.back: It helps distribute requests/data efficiently and evenly across servers while minimizing remapping when the server set changes.

flashcards.front: What is the traditional modulo hashing formula?
flashcards.back: serverIndex = hash(key) % N.

flashcards.front: What does N represent in hash(key) % N?
flashcards.back: The number of servers in the server pool.

flashcards.front: When does modulo hashing work well?
flashcards.back: When the server-pool size is fixed and the data distribution is even.

flashcards.front: Why does modulo hashing fail badly when a server is removed?
flashcards.back: N changes, so the modulo result changes for many keys even though their original hash values do not.

flashcards.front: What operational problem can widespread remapping cause in a cache cluster?
flashcards.back: A storm of cache misses because clients look for keys on newly computed servers where the data is not cached.

flashcards.front: In the four-server example, where does key0 map?
flashcards.back: server1 because hash(key0) % 4 = 1.

flashcards.front: In the four-server example, which keys map to server0?
flashcards.back: key1 and key3.

flashcards.front: In the four-server example, which keys map to server1?
flashcards.back: key0 and key4.

flashcards.front: In the four-server example, which keys map to server2?
flashcards.back: key2 and key6.

flashcards.front: In the four-server example, which keys map to server3?
flashcards.back: key5 and key7.

flashcards.front: What happens to the modulo divisor if one of four servers fails?
flashcards.back: It changes from 4 to 3.

flashcards.front: What does the chapter say about how many keys consistent hashing remaps when resized?
flashcards.back: Only about k/n keys on average, where k is the number of keys and n is the number of slots.

flashcards.front: What SHA-1 hash-space range does the chapter use?
flashcards.back: 0 through 2^160 - 1.

flashcards.front: How is a hash ring formed conceptually?
flashcards.back: By connecting the two ends of the linear hash space.

flashcards.front: How are servers placed on the ring?
flashcards.back: Hash the server IP or name using the same hash function and place the result on the ring.

flashcards.front: How are keys placed on the ring?
flashcards.back: Hash the keys into the same hash space and place them at those positions.

flashcards.front: Does the ring-based approach use hash(key) % N for lookup?
flashcards.back: No. The chapter explicitly notes there is no modular operation in the consistent-hashing lookup.

flashcards.front: How do you find a key's server?
flashcards.back: Move clockwise from the key until the first server is encountered.

flashcards.front: In Figure 5-7, where is key0 stored?
flashcards.back: server0.

flashcards.front: In Figure 5-7, where is key1 stored?
flashcards.back: server1.

flashcards.front: In Figure 5-7, where is key2 stored?
flashcards.back: server2.

flashcards.front: In Figure 5-7, where is key3 stored?
flashcards.back: server3.

flashcards.front: What is the main effect of adding a server under consistent hashing?
flashcards.back: Only a fraction of keys need redistribution.

flashcards.front: When server4 is added in the chapter, which key moves?
flashcards.back: Only key0.

flashcards.front: Why does key0 move from server0 to server4?
flashcards.back: server4 becomes the first server encountered clockwise from key0.

flashcards.front: When server1 is removed, which key moves?
flashcards.back: Only key1.

flashcards.front: Where does key1 move after server1 is removed?
flashcards.back: server2.

flashcards.front: What are the two basic problems of the naïve ring?
flashcards.back: Unequal partition sizes and non-uniform key distribution.

flashcards.front: What is a partition on the ring?
flashcards.back: The hash-space interval between adjacent servers.

flashcards.front: What unequal-partition example does the chapter give?
flashcards.back: After s1 is removed, s2's partition becomes twice as large as s0's and s3's partitions.

flashcards.front: What non-uniform distribution example does the chapter give?
flashcards.back: Most keys can land on server2 while server1 and server3 have no data.

flashcards.front: What technique solves the two basic ring problems?
flashcards.back: Virtual nodes, also called replicas.

flashcards.front: What is a virtual node?
flashcards.back: A ring position that refers to a real server; each real server is represented by multiple virtual nodes.

flashcards.front: How many virtual nodes per server are shown in the example?
flashcards.back: Three, though the chapter says this is arbitrary and real systems use many more.

flashcards.front: What are server0's virtual-node names in the example?
What are server1's virtual-node names in the example?
How is a key assigned when virtual nodes are used?
flashcards.back: Move clockwise from the key to the first virtual node; the real server represented by that virtual node owns the key.

flashcards.front: Which virtual node owns k0 in Figure 5-13?
flashcards.back: s1_1, which refers to server1.

flashcards.front: What happens to key distribution as the number of virtual nodes increases?
flashcards.back: It becomes more balanced.

flashcards.front: Why does more virtual nodes improve balance according to the chapter?
flashcards.back: The standard deviation of the distribution becomes smaller.

flashcards.front: What standard-deviation examples does the chapter cite?
flashcards.back: About 10% of the mean at 100 virtual nodes and about 5% at 200 virtual nodes.

flashcards.front: What is the cost of increasing the number of virtual nodes?
flashcards.back: More space is required to store virtual-node metadata.

flashcards.front: How do you find the affected range when adding a server?
flashcards.back: Start at the new server and move anticlockwise to the previous server; keys in that interval move to the new server.

flashcards.front: When s4 is added, what range is affected?
flashcards.back: The range between s3 and s4.

flashcards.front: How do you find the affected range when removing a server?
flashcards.back: Start at the removed server's former position and move anticlockwise to the previous server; that interval's keys move to the next server clockwise.

flashcards.front: When s1 is removed, what range is affected?
flashcards.back: The range between s0 and s1.

flashcards.front: Where do keys between s0 and removed s1 move?
flashcards.back: To s2.

flashcards.front: What are the three benefits listed in the wrap-up?
flashcards.back: Minimized redistribution, easier horizontal scaling from more even distribution, and mitigation of hotspot-key problems.

flashcards.front: How can consistent hashing help hotspot problems?
flashcards.back: By spreading data more evenly so heavily accessed data is less likely to concentrate on a single shard.

flashcards.front: Which Amazon system is listed as using consistent hashing?
flashcards.back: Dynamo.

flashcards.front: Which distributed database besides Dynamo is listed?
flashcards.back: Apache Cassandra.

flashcards.front: Which chat application is listed as a real-world use?
flashcards.back: Discord.

flashcards.front: Which CDN is listed?
flashcards.back: Akamai.

flashcards.front: Which network load balancer is listed?
flashcards.back: Maglev.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does modulo hashing cause widespread remapping when N changes?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The hash values themselves stay the same, but the modulo divisor changes. Because hash(key) % N depends directly on N, many keys produce different server indexes after a server is added or removed.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the operational consequence of that remapping in a cache cluster?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Clients compute new server locations for many keys, but those keys are not actually cached there yet, causing a large number of cache misses.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the core lookup rule of consistent hashing.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Servers and keys are hashed into the same circular hash space. Starting from a key's position, the first server encountered while moving clockwise owns that key.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does adding a server require only limited redistribution?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Only keys in the interval that now encounter the new server before their previous owner change ownership. Other keys still encounter the same first server clockwise.

short_answer_questions.question: What are the two limitations of the basic consistent-hashing ring?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The server partitions can have very different sizes, and key distribution can be non-uniform, causing some servers to hold many keys while others hold few or none.

short_answer_questions.question: How do virtual nodes improve distribution?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Each real server is represented by multiple positions around the ring, so it owns several smaller partitions rather than one large contiguous interval. Increasing the number of virtual nodes reduces distribution variance.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the virtual-node tradeoff?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: More virtual nodes improve load balance by reducing standard deviation, but storing information about more virtual nodes requires additional space.

short_answer_questions.question: How are affected keys identified when adding a node?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Start from the new node and move anticlockwise until the previous server is found. Keys in the interval between that previous server and the new server must move to the new server.

short_answer_questions.question: How are affected keys identified when removing a node?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Start at the removed node's former position and move anticlockwise to the previous server. The keys in that interval must be reassigned to the next server clockwise.

short_answer_questions.question: What benefits does the chapter list in its wrap-up?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Minimize key redistribution, make horizontal scaling easier through more even distribution, and mitigate hotspot-key problems.

common_confusions.correction: The chapter explicitly notes that the ring-based lookup does not use the modulo operation.

common_confusions.confusion: The nearest server in either direction owns a key.
common_confusions.correction: Ownership is determined by the first server encountered while moving clockwise.

common_confusions.confusion: The basic hash ring automatically balances load perfectly.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter identifies unequal partitions and non-uniform key distribution as two basic-ring problems.

common_confusions.confusion: A virtual node is an additional physical server.
common_confusions.correction: A virtual node refers to a real server; one physical server can have many virtual positions on the ring.

common_confusions.confusion: More virtual nodes are always free.
common_confusions.correction: More virtual nodes improve balance but consume additional space for virtual-node metadata.

common_confusions.confusion: Affected keys after adding a server are found by moving clockwise to the next server.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter identifies the affected range by starting at the new server and moving anticlockwise to the previous server.

common_confusions.confusion: Consistent hashing is only a caching technique.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter lists use in database partitioning, cluster partitioning, chat infrastructure, CDNs, and network load balancing.

practice_problems.prompt: A cluster has 5 servers and a key hash is 47. Which server index does modulo hashing select?
practice_problems.note: New practice question based on the chapter's modulo-hashing formula.

practice_problems.prompt: The same key hash 47 is remapped after one server is removed and N changes from 5 to 4. What server index is selected now?
practice_problems.answer: 47 % 4 = 3. The key changes from server2 to server3, illustrating the rehashing problem.
practice_problems.note: New practice question based on the chapter's rehashing problem.

practice_problems.prompt: Servers occur clockwise at ring positions 10, 40, 70, and 90. A key hashes to position 68. Which server owns it?
practice_problems.answer: The server at 70, because it is the first server encountered clockwise.
practice_problems.note: New practice question based on the chapter's lookup rule.

practice_problems.prompt: Servers are at positions 10, 40, and 70. A key hashes to 95 on a circular 0-99 ring. Which server owns it?
practice_problems.answer: The server at 10 after wrapping around the ring.
practice_problems.note: New practice question based on the circular hash-ring model.

practice_problems.prompt: Why might representing a server with 100 virtual nodes be better balanced than representing it with one ring position?
practice_problems.answer: The server receives multiple smaller partitions distributed around the ring, reducing distribution variance; the tradeoff is more vnode metadata.
practice_problems.note: New practice question based on the chapter's virtual-node discussion.

must_memorize: Modulo hashing is stable only while N remains fixed.
Changing N remaps many keys and can cause a cache-miss storm.
Consistent hashing remaps only a fraction of keys when membership changes.
Connect both ends of the hash space to form a ring.
Hash servers and keys into the same ring.
A key belongs to the first server encountered clockwise.
Adding a server moves only keys in the neighboring affected interval.
Removing a server moves only the affected interval to the next clockwise server.
Basic-ring problems: unequal partition sizes and non-uniform key distribution.
Virtual nodes represent one real server at many ring positions.
More virtual nodes usually mean better balance and lower standard deviation.
More virtual nodes also require more metadata/storage.
For an added server, find the affected range by moving anticlockwise to the previous server.
For a removed server, find the affected interval similarly and move it to the next server clockwise.
Benefits: minimized redistribution, easier horizontal scaling, hotspot mitigation.
Examples listed: Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai, Maglev.
chapter_five_final_review.memory_chain: MODULO PROBLEM -> HASH SPACE -> HASH RING -> HASH SERVERS + KEYS -> CLOCKWISE LOOKUP -> LIMITED REMAPPING -> BASIC RING IMBALANCE -> VIRTUAL NODES -> AFFECTED KEY RANGES
chapter_five_final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: Consistent hashing decouples key placement from the exact server count by assigning keys within a circular hash space, so server membership changes move only neighboring ranges of keys; virtual nodes then make that distribution substantially more balanced.
